top_choice_rationale: P001 (Kiyotaki and Moore, B002) is the most defensible award on the slate. The 1997 paper is a two-author origin of one original general-equilibrium mechanism, in which borrowing limits tied to collateral values feed back on asset prices and credit so that temporary shocks become persistent and amplified. It has almost three decades of use in macro-finance, quantitative macro and policy modelling. Credit is the cleanest on the shortlist, since no originator is left out of the two-name set. The Gertler and Gilchrist accelerator strand is a different, broader citation. The 2022 prize on banks and runs concerns a distinct mechanism, so the overlap is a balance question and not duplicated merit. The main weakness is that the quantitative size of collateral amplification is identified less cleanly than the theory's influence suggests. I rank P002 (Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn, B012) second. It is mature and widely used, and a narrowly worded demand-estimation citation is defensible. Its attribution gap (Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin) and its structural-assumption dependence keep it below P001. I rank no award last because both proposals are substantive, mature achievements.
recusal_note: No connection to the credited names of B002 or B012 is apparent from the profile; none of my listed co-authors is credited. I co-authored a 2026 IJIO paper with chair John Hassler and former chair Tore Ellingsen, who are colleagues and not candidates. Hassler also prefers B002, so I do not treat his agreement as independent confirmation. My IO and pricing research is adjacent to B012, and I discount any affinity for it. My spouse, Magdalena Andersson, is a public fact, and I found no evidence it bears on these candidates. I do not treat it as a conflict. Disclosed without adjudication.
